- No account switching, no login flow, no second account read; the card names the login already in use and nothing more.
- No id token is decoded and no extra request is made to learn an identity.

## Phase 185 — the diff view chooses how a change is drawn (operator asked 2026-08-31, BEFORE THE RELEASE) SHIPPED 2026-08-31

**Subject:** `feat(diff): the diff view chooses its inline highlighting and its backgrounds`
**First body line:** `Phase 185: your diffs, your choice`
**Semver:** minor.
**Tier 2**, one app run driving every mode over a real diff, one named independent method.
**Charter:** his words and screenshot of 2026-08-31, wanting enhanced word and character level diffing and a switch for background colouring, configured IN THE DIFF VIEW of the file rather than buried in Settings, the way Pierre's own product already offers it.

### The mechanism is already in the bundle, measured before this was queued
`@pierre/diffs` 1.3.5 is already a dependency and its own type at `node_modules/@pierre/diffs/dist/types.d.ts:335` reads:
`type LineDiffTypes = 'word-alt' | 'word' | 'char' | 'none'`
and Tortie already passes one of them, HARD CODED, at `src/renderer/pierre/diff-render-options.ts:24`, being `lineDiffType: 'word' as LineDiffTypes`. So the four modes in his screenshot are not new work and not a new package: they are a constant that needs to become a choice. **CONFIRM THIS AGAINST THE TREE FIRST ANYWAY**, and confirm what each mode actually draws rather than trusting the names, because word-alt is described by Pierre as an enhanced algorithm and the phase should say plainly what the difference looks like on a real hunk.

### What it builds
- **A control IN THE DIFF VIEW**, at the head of the diff surface where the file is being read, not in Settings. His screenshot is the shape to learn from, not to copy: a small row of controls that belong to the thing they change.
- **Inline highlighting**: the four Pierre modes, with a plain word for each. The default stays what ships today so nobody's diffs change under them without asking.
- **Backgrounds on or off**: the full width change colouring toggles, which is a Tortie styling decision rather than a Pierre option, so establish where that colour is applied before deciding whether it is a class on the surface or an option passed down.
- **The choice PERSISTS** and applies to every diff, because a per file choice that resets is an annoyance rather than a setting. Where it is stored is the phase's call, and it is one setting, not a per project one.
- Under Just enough words: a short label per control, the detail on hover, no paragraph explaining what word-alt is on the resting face.
- Colours from tokens.css only, and the existing diff theme bridge is not bypassed.

### Proof, run rather than read
- One app run over a REAL diff carrying a line with several small changes in it, photographing all four inline modes and both background states, and proving the drawn spans actually differ between word, word-alt and char rather than the option being accepted and ignored.
- THE NAMED INDEPENDENT METHOD: re-derive what changed by a different route, being an own diff of the same hunk computed independently, and prove the highlighted ranges in char mode really are the changed characters and in word mode really are the changed words. An option that is passed but not honoured looks identical to one that works until somebody checks the spans.
- The choice survives a reload and applies to a diff opened afterwards.
- DRIVE THE WHOLE JOURNEY, the lesson from Phases 175, 181 and 174.1: change each control while a diff is OPEN and prove the view follows at once rather than only on the next open.
- The battery.

### What is NOT in this phase
- No new package and no new renderer; the modes are Pierre's own and already bundled.
- No line wrapping, line number or bars-versus-classic controls, whatever his screenshot shows; those are Pierre product features and each is its own decision.
- No per file or per project memory of the choice.
- No change to the diff theme, the token colours or the highlight pool.

## Phase 186 — the website learns what shipped (operator asked 2026-08-31, AFTER the release, DRAFT ONLY) SHIPPED 2026-09-01

**Subject:** `docs(site): the release and its features reach the website`
**First body line:** `Phase 186: the website learns what shipped`
**Semver:** none. This phase touches NO code in this repository; it works in `/Users/gdc/tortiedotsh`.
**Tier 1**, because it is copy and data. The gates are the site's own build and whatever check that repository already runs.
**Charter:** his words of 2026-08-31, after the release is cut: update the changelog on the website and add the relevant product documentation for what shipped, draft it, and COMMIT IT AS ONE COMMIT HE CAN REVIEW. **DO NOT PUSH.** He reads it in the morning.

### The two rules that bind this phase absolutely
1. **ONE COMMIT, and it is NOT PUSHED.** Everything lands as a single reviewable commit in `/Users/gdc/tortiedotsh` on whatever branch is checked out. No push, no tag, no PR, no deploy. Say the hash so he can find it.
2. **HIS WORKING TREE IS HIS.** That checkout carries his own uncommitted work, including an edited Hero.astro and demo files at the time of writing. NEVER commit, stash, revert or discard anything he changed. Commit ONLY the files this phase writes, by explicit path, never `git add -A` or `git add .`. If a file this phase must touch already has his uncommitted edits in it, STOP and say so rather than folding his work into your commit.

### What it writes, read from the tree rather than assumed
- **The changelog.** `src/data/changelog.json` is an object with `sourceUrl` and `releases`, an array whose newest entry is 0.76.1 dated 2026-08-26 with `version`, `date`, `summary` and `sections`, each section a `title` and `items` of `text`. Add ONE entry for the release that was just cut, in that exact shape, newest first. CLAUDE.md's release rule says the site carries the CHANGELOG entry VERBATIM, so the text comes from the repository's own CHANGELOG.md rather than being rewritten; reconcile the shape, never the words.
- **The product documentation.** `src/data/docs.ts` is a typed tree of sections and pages, about 1,172 lines, with groups Start, Core concepts, Work with Tortie and Reference. The features this release adds need to be findable by somebody who never read the changelog. Decide from the tree where each belongs rather than inventing a new group: the subscription usage meters and the custom terminal font sit near Settings and customization; the diff view controls sit near Files, search and previews or Source control; Oh My Pi belongs in Supported agents, which may already name it; Architecture behind its Settings flag needs a page that says plainly that it is off until a person turns it on and why.
- Every page follows the shapes already in that file, being paragraphs, notes, steps and lists, and its house voice. NO em dashes or en dashes. Write what a person can do, not how it was built.

### What it must get right
- **Say the limits.** The meters are off by default per provider and only Claude and Codex are read; a custom font is not inlined into a capture so a captured session renders in Menlo; Architecture is off by default and most agents cannot fill in a contract yet. A documentation page that omits a limit a person will hit in the first hour is worse than no page.
- **Nothing is invented.** If a feature's behaviour is not in the CHANGELOG entry or readable in the gmux tree, it is not written down. Check anything uncertain against `/Users/gdc/gmux` READ ONLY.
- **The build passes.** Run whatever the site repository's own build or check command is before committing, and say what was run.

### What is NOT in this phase
- No push, no deploy, no release page on the site, no tag.
- No redesign of the docs tree, no new top level group unless the tree makes one unavoidable, and no change to unrelated pages.
- No change to anything in the gmux repository.
- No touching his uncommitted work in that checkout, for any reason.

## Phase 187 — a closed remote tab stays closed (operator reported 2026-08-31) SHIPPED 2026-09-01

**Subject:** `fix(machines): closing a remote session closes it for good`
**First body line:** `Phase 187: the tab that comes back`
**Semver:** patch unless the cause turns out to be in durable state, which earns more.
**Tier 3.** It is session lifecycle on a remote machine, which is the person's real work, and the CLAUDE.md tier rule says anything that can lose or corrupt work is Tier 3. He reported it personally, so the PARENT COMMIT MEASUREMENT IS MANDATORY.
**Charter:** his words of 2026-08-31: closing a remote machine tab tends to bring it back at least once, and he does not know why. He calls it a bug and he is right to; a close that does not stay closed is the app disagreeing with him about his own work.

### REPRODUCE FIRST. DO NOT FIX A THEORY.
The symptom is INTERMITTENT and that is the most important fact in this entry. **At least once** means it comes back sometimes and not always, so a single close that behaves proves nothing and a fix validated by one close is not validated. Establish a REPEATABLE reproduction with a count before touching any code: close a remote session N times and record how many came back, on his own machine shape. A phase that cannot reproduce it says so and stops rather than changing code on a guess.

### The candidates, named so no round re-derives them, each to be confirmed or killed against the tree
The remote layer has several things that can put a row back, and any of them fits an intermittent return.
1. **A poll completing after the close.** `src/main/machines/remote-sessions.ts` reads sessions from a live feed or a list, and its own header records a 5,000 ms list cadence. A list that was IN FLIGHT when the close happened returns afterwards holding the session it saw before, and whatever consumes it puts the row back. This is the first candidate and the one the timing fits.
2. **The close did not reach the far side.** If Tortie removed the row locally but the tmux session on the machine is still alive, the next completed list correctly reports it and the row is right to come back. Then the defect is in the close, not the reconcile. Distinguish these two by asking the far machine directly whether the session still exists after a close, READ ONLY.
3. **The store sync.** `src/main/machines/remote-store-sync.ts` runs on a 300,000 ms cadence. A slower loop rewriting state from a snapshot taken before the close would return a row minutes later rather than seconds later, which is a DIFFERENT symptom in time; measure WHEN the row returns, because that number alone separates candidates 1 and 3.
4. **The reconcile judgement.** The same file's header says a kill or a rename is composed only against an identifier a completed poll saw, and that a failed list is judged rather than trusted. Read that rule and check whether a close races it.
5. **The renderer.** The row may never leave main's truth at all and only the surface removed it, so any refresh redraws it. Check whether main's own state still holds the session after a close.
**MEASURE WHEN IT COMES BACK**, in seconds after the close, and that measurement chooses the candidate before any code is read closely.

### REPRODUCED, 2026-08-31, and the candidate is named (the reproduce round)

`npm run probe:p187` is the reproduction. It stands up its own loopback sshd with its own keys and its own ssh agent, exactly as Phase 173 established, confirms and prepares that machine through the product's own bridge, and closes remote sessions many times over one app run, reading MAIN'S OWN LIST through `sessions:list` rather than a photograph. His Mac Pro was never contacted. His own server read 52 sessions before every run and 52 after.

#### The count, which is the thing the entry asked for first

| Drive | Closes | Came back | Far machine still held the session |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| the x on a live session, `sessions:kill`, loopback | 25 | 0 | 0 |
| that close plus the second click, `sessions:discard`, loopback | 25 | 0 | 0 |
| the same two, with every tmux command on the machine behind a 300 ms wait | 40 | 0 | 0 |
| a project tab whose folder is on the machine | 25 | 0 | not applicable |
| the same id in BOTH of main's maps, then one Remove | 5 | **5** | not applicable |

**Ninety ordinary closes returned nothing, and the ninety first shape returned every time.** There is no distribution to report for the ordinary close, because nothing came back at any delay: a 420 second tail watch over all forty ids closed in one run recorded zero sightings, which is longer than the 300,000 ms store sync cadence and settles candidate 3 without reading a line of it.

#### The far machine was asked directly after every close, and it always answered the same

Read only, over that machine's own ssh, `list-sessions` alone. Ninety closes, ninety answers, and the machine held the session after NONE of them. **Candidate 2 is dead.** The close reaches the far side, so a row that comes back is a stale row rather than a correct report of a session that is still alive, and the fix is not in the close.

#### The one shape that reproduces it, five times out of five

Main holds two maps per machine in `src/main/machines/remote-sessions.ts`, being `state.rows` for what the last completed list reported and `state.gone` for a row that list stopped reporting. Put the SAME id in both, press the person's Remove, and the row is still in main's own list three seconds later reading `idle`. Press Remove a second time and it goes. That is his sentence, being that closing it brings it back AT LEAST ONCE, reproduced as a number.

The line is `forgetRemoteRow`, which `removeSession` in `src/main/sessions/core.ts` calls for every remote row:

```
if (state.gone.delete(sessionId) || state.rows.delete(sessionId)) {
```

`||` short circuits. When the id is in BOTH maps the first delete answers true and **`state.rows.delete` never runs**, so the row stays in main's truth and every redraw brings the tab back. The second Remove works because `gone` is empty by then, so the second delete is the one that runs. The ordinary Remove arm, twenty five closes with the id in one map only, cleared the row every time, so the two arms differ in exactly the thing this line reads.

#### How an id comes to be in both maps, which is what makes it intermittent

Nothing ever removes an id from `gone`. `onePass` puts a row there when a completed list stops reporting it and then replaces `state.rows` wholesale, so a session that goes away and COMES BACK UNDER THE SAME `@gmux-id` lands in `rows` while its old `gone` entry is still sitting there. Tortie's own remote restore does exactly that: `src/main/machines/remote-restore.ts` stamps `'@gmux-id': sessionId` on the session it recreates. So a remote session that was ended or lost and then restored is in both maps for the rest of the run.

#### What that leaves for the fix round, stated as an open question rather than a guess

`remoteRecordStatus` reads `rows` before `gone`, so a row in both maps READS live, and the x offers End rather than Remove for a live row. The reproduction therefore reached Remove through `sessions:discard` directly, which is the same channel the person's Remove uses and is what `removeSession` in the renderer calls, but at a moment the resting surface would have offered End. The remaining question is which gesture puts a person on Remove while main has the row in both maps, and the two candidates are a renderer snapshot that still says ended when the click is handled, and a row with no live manifest row, which `remoteSessions` pushes TWICE when it is in both maps. **Neither of those needs to be answered before the short circuit is fixed**, because a Remove must clear the row from both maps whatever put it in them.

#### What the other candidates are, now that they are measured

- **Candidate 1, a poll completing after the close: not the cause on its own.** Every command on the machine has the same round trip, and `remoteKill` runs a list of its own AFTER the kill, so a list issued before the kill always completes before that one. Ninety closes at two latencies produced no return. It is still the thing that widens the window, because a stale list is one of the two ways a row lands back in `rows`.
- **Candidate 2, the close never reached the far side: dead.** Asked directly, ninety times.
- **Candidate 3, the 300,000 ms store sync: dead.** A 420 second tail over forty closed ids recorded zero sightings, and `src/main/machines/remote-store-sync.ts` copies conversation files and holds no session row.
- **Candidate 4, the reconcile judgement racing the close: not seen.** The rule holds in the measurement: a kill is composed only against an identifier a completed list reported, and every one of the ninety closes landed on the far machine.
- **Candidate 5, main's truth never losing the row: THIS IS IT**, and the entry's wording was right. Main keeps the row, and the surface is only reporting what main hands it.

#### Two smaller things the run measured, recorded so nobody re-derives them

- The machine is on the LIVE CONNECTION rather than the 5,000 ms list. An out of band kill on the far side was noticed by main in 242 ms on loopback and 451 ms with the 300 ms wait, so "seconds after the close" would have pointed at the connection rather than at the list even if something had come back.
- A closed session that is not on any machine behaves the same: five local closes left the row in main's list five times, reading `exited`. **A tab staying on screen after End is shipped behaviour and is not this defect**, and a fix round must not "fix" it.

### FIXED, 2026-09-01, at the cause, with the parent measured (the fix round)

The cause was re-derived from the tree before a line was changed, and the reproduce round was right.
The fix is two lines in two places, both in `src/main/machines/remote-sessions.ts`, and it landed as
`2e9650c`.

**The pass now takes an id OUT of `gone`.** A completed list holding the session is proof it is not
gone, and until this commit nothing ever removed an id from that map while `state.rows` was replaced
wholesale. That is the line that keeps the two maps DISJOINT, and it is what ends the second defect
nobody had named: `remoteSessions` pushed a row in both maps twice, once live and once proven absent,
so one session drew as two rows.

**A Remove clears BOTH maps.** `forgetRemoteRow` no longer reads
`state.gone.delete(id) || state.rows.delete(id)`, whose `||` short circuited so `state.rows.delete`
never ran. A Remove is the person saying the row is finished, so it clears whatever holds it.

Nothing is sent to any machine by either line, no cadence moved and no durable state was touched, so
the semver is patch as the entry allowed for. `remoteRowsInBothMaps` is the new counter beside
`machinesWithBothFeeds`, and it must always be empty.

#### The guard, and the parent measurement it was taken against

`npm run conformance:remoteclose` drives the real feed over **25 closes per arm** with the exec plane
replaced by a function. It spawns nothing at all, starts no ssh, opens no manifest and launches no
Electron, in about 0.6 s, so it is cheap enough for the commit battery beside `npm run probe:p187`,
which is the same drive over a loopback machine and takes minutes. It is named in `package.json`,
classified in `build/verification-checks.mjs` and written into CLAUDE.md's gate list.

| Arm | What it drives, 25 times | At the parent | At HEAD |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Remove after the session was restored under the same id | **25 of 25 came back** | 0 |
| B | the x on a live row, then Remove | 0 | 0 |
| C | Remove on a row a completed list stopped reporting | 0 | 0 |
| D | one id churned through 25 disappearances and returns | **25 of 25 in both maps, 25 of 25 drawn twice** | 0 and 0 |
| E | the SECOND Remove, which must find nothing | **25 of 25 still found it** | 0 |
| F | a Remove naming no row still answers false | passes | passes |

Arms B, C and F pass at the parent as well, which is what says the gate is not trivially red.

#### THE REPRODUCTION ITSELF, RE-RUN AT HEAD

`npm run probe:p187 -- --trials 5 --tail 20000` was run at HEAD on its own loopback sshd with its own
keys and its own agent, his Mac Pro never contacted, his own server read 54 sessions before and 54
after. **The GHOST arm, which returned 5 of 5 at the parent, is 0 of 5 at HEAD**: after ONE Remove the
row is GONE every time, so no second Remove was needed and `stillListedAfterSecondRemove` is null on
every trial. Everything else is unchanged, which is the point: END 0 of 5, REMOVE 0 of 5, the far
machine held the session after none of them, the 20 s tail over all 10 closed ids recorded 0
sightings, calibration 240 ms so the machine is still on the live connection, the LOCAL control still
leaves 5 of 5 rows listed reading `exited` because a tab staying on screen after End is shipped
behaviour, and the project arm's one sighting is the same sub 250 ms render lag at 9 ms with main
never holding the row. Report: `head-ghost.json` beside the reproduce round's own cohort files.

### FIXED AGAIN, 2026-09-01, at the candidate the first round left open (the second fix round)

The first round fixed the shape that returns EVERY time and did not fix the shape
a person actually meets. Candidate 1 was still open, and it is the defect.

**The honest product timeline.** A status list goes out at T. The person presses
the x at T+5 ms and Remove at T+10 ms, and `forgetRemoteRow` clears both maps, so
main's truth no longer holds the row. The machine answers at T+60 ms with the
membership it had BEFORE the close, and `onePass` writes `state.rows = seen` with
nothing comparing that answer's age against the moment of the Remove. The row is
back, the next pass moves it to `gone` reading `restorable`, ten passes later it
is still drawn, and a second Remove is what shifts it.

**Measured before a line was changed, over 200 lives with one Remove each**, the
real feed driven with the exec plane replaced by a function: 200 of 200 came back,
200 of 200 were still drawn ten passes later, and the second Remove found it 200
of 200 times. **The same 200 at the first round's parent**, so the two lines that
round shipped neither caused this nor cured it, and it was never a regression.

It is user visible rather than main only. `SessionCore.listSessions` skips a
discarded manifest row BEFORE `covered.add(rec.id)` at `src/main/sessions/core.ts`,
so the Remove tombstones the record and the reinstated feed row is then pushed
uncovered and draws a tab.

**The fix is one rule.** A pass whose `snapshotAt` predates a Remove may not
reinstate the id that Remove cleared. `forgetRemoteRow` stamps the instant of the
Remove per session id and `onePass` drops those ids from `seen` before anything
reads it. `snapshotAt` is stamped before the command is issued, so a list issued
AFTER the Remove is a fresh answer and is trusted in full: a Remove is not a kill
and nothing here makes a session on that machine permanently invisible. A tie goes
to the person, because `Date.now()` has millisecond granularity and a list issued
in the same millisecond cannot have seen the close; with a strict comparison 194 of
the 200 lives still came back. The instants are pruned at twice the list timeout,
which is a bound rather than a taste, and `state.names` is deliberately untouched
because the session may still be running on that machine under that name.

#### The guard grew five arms, and each part of the fix has one that fails for it

| Arm | What it drives | Ablated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| G | the timeline above, 25 times | drop the removal instant: **25 of 25 came back** |
| H | a list issued AFTER the Remove is still believed | the rule would make a live session invisible |
| I | the removal instants are forgotten, so nothing grows | the map would grow for the whole run |
| J | two rows closed in one tick under one list in flight | drop the removal instant: fails |
| K | the belt, an id in both maps by a route that is not a pass | restore the `||`: **25 of 25 came back** |

**Arm K is why `overlapRemoteRowForTests` exists, and it answers a real weakness in
the first round.** Once the pass keeps the two maps disjoint there is no route
through the feed that puts an id in both, so the belt in `forgetRemoteRow` could
have been deleted with every gate still green. That was ablated and confirmed: with
the `||` restored, arms A to J all passed. The seam puts an id in both by the same
route the ghost arm of `probe:p187` used on the real app.

#### THE REAL DATA PROOF, and the parent measured on the real app

`npm run probe:p187` grew an arm called RACE. A session settles live on the loopback
machine, a second session appears there out of band so main issues a list that holds
the first, the x is fired and NOT awaited because `remoteKill` announces the row as
ended before it awaits its own poll, the probe waits for main's own list to read the
row as ended, and Remove is pressed while the list from before the close is still on
the wire. `--slow-list` makes the LIST alone slow on the machine, which is a far side
slow to answer one question; `--slow` cannot do this, because it slows the End and
the poll behind it too and the close never lands inside the window.

**The first version of that wrapper slept and then listed, and the arm passed at the
parent because of it.** A late list describes the machine at the moment it finally
ran, so it holds no session the close had already ended. The defect is an answer that
is STALE rather than late, so the list runs at once, its output is held, and the
DELIVERY waits. The arm also proves its own window rather than assuming it: the
second session is stamped like a Tortie session, so the instant main first lists it
IS the instant the held list answered, and every trial records that number and fails
itself if the held list had already answered.

| | at the parent | at HEAD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| came back when the held list landed | **3 of 3** | 0 of 5 |
| still there after the passes | **3 of 3, reading `restorable`** | 0 of 5 |
| the second Remove is what shifted it | yes, every trial | never needed |
| the held list answered, after the Remove | 3,997 to 4,008 ms | 3,967 to 4,125 ms |

Everything else in the run is unchanged: GHOST 0 of 5, END 0 of 5, REMOVE 0 of 5, the
far machine held the session after none of the closes, a tail over every closed id
recorded 0 sightings, calibration 239 ms so the machine is still on the live
connection, the LOCAL control still leaves 5 of 5 rows listed reading `exited`, and
the project arm's one sighting is the same sub 250 ms render lag with main never
holding the row. His own server read 54 sessions before and 54 after every run.

#### A stray from the first round's own probe, and the rule it broke

A scratch ssh agent from `probe:p187` was found still running hours later, pid 59110,
`/usr/bin/ssh-agent -s`, started inside that probe's window and holding that run's
throwaway key. The probe was not careless: it records the agent pid, its teardown
kills every recorded pid, and that teardown is in a `finally`. The gap is structural,
because `scratchYard` is called at MODULE LEVEL above the `try` that `finally`
belongs to, so anything that ends the process before the `try` is entered leaves the
agent behind. Every caller of that module has the same shape. Measured: a harness that
stands up a yard and then throws left the agent and its socket directory behind at the
parent and leaves nothing at HEAD, over both the `-s` and the `-a` shapes. The agent
now ends on `exit`, with SIGTERM so ssh-agent can remove its own socket, and the
socket is removed only after `lstatSync` proves it IS a socket. The three probes that
start an agent outside the yard call the same function rather than growing a fourth
copy. Pid 59110 was NOT killed: it is not this session's, and it is reported rather
than acted on.

#### What is still open, unchanged from both fix rounds

`remoteRecordStatus` reads `rows` before `gone`, so a row in both maps READ live and the x offered
End rather than Remove. Which gesture put a person on Remove in that state is still unanswered. One
of its two candidates, the double push the projection made for such a row, is gone with this commit.

### Proof, run rather than read
- THE REPRODUCTION with a count at the parent commit, being N closes and the number that returned, and the same drive at HEAD showing zero returns over at least the same N. An intermittent defect needs repetition to be called fixed, and one clean close is not evidence.
- The far machine is asked directly, READ ONLY, whether the session survives a close, so the phase knows which of candidates 1 and 2 it fixed.
- THE NAMED INDEPENDENT METHOD: re-derive the row's life from the RAW facts rather than the product's verdict, being the completed list output and main's own state at each step, and show where the returning row enters. The verifier does this by its own reading, not by the phase's logging.
- A guard that CAN FAIL: whatever check ships must go red at the parent and green at HEAD, and be named in package.json and build/verification-checks.mjs. Two phases shipped unreachable or unfailable guards this week.
- The battery plus npm run conformance:machines.

### The safety rules this phase inherits and cannot bend
- His remote machines are HIS. The harness starts its OWN loopback sshd with its OWN keys, exactly as Phase 173 established; his Mac Pro is READ ONLY and is never contacted for a test. His ssh agent holds no identities and stays that way, and ~/.ssh is never touched.
- Only ever the gmux socket read only. Never kill a session on his server. A scratch server lives on its own socket and is ended in a finally.
- If the reproduction genuinely needs a real remote machine and loopback cannot stand in, the phase STOPS and records what he would have to provide.

### What is NOT in this phase
- No redesign of the remote feed, the poll cadence or the store sync.
- No change to what a close does on the far machine beyond making it stick.
- No new setting, and no user-visible copy unless the fix needs a line saying a close is in flight.

## Phase 188 — the sessions table says whose work each row is (operator asked 2026-08-31)

**Subject:** `feat(diagnostics): the sessions table names the project and the age`
**First body line:** `Phase 188: whose work, and since when`
**Semver:** minor. New columns on an existing surface.
**Tier 2**, one app run driving every claim, one named independent method. He reported it, so the parent measurement is mandatory.
**Charter:** his words and screenshot of 2026-08-31, wanting the usage report to say which project each session is actually in, and detail about when it was first started and last active.

### Why the table is unreadable today, from his own screenshot
It lists 184 processes across dozens of rows and the names REPEAT: five separate rows read `claude-1`, four read `claude-2`, four read `codex-1`. Those are different sessions in different projects sharing a per project counter, so the identifying part of the name is missing from the table. A row holding 3,226 MB cannot be traced to the work it belongs to, which is the whole reason a person opens this pane.

### The facts already exist, measured before this was queued, so this is plumbing rather than new measurement
`src/main/manifest/schema.ts` already stores, per session: `project_path`, `cwd`, `agent`, `created_at` and `last_seen`, with an index on `project_path`. Nothing new has to be observed, sampled or spawned. CONFIRM THIS AGAINST THE TREE FIRST, then read what the diagnostics report already carries per session and join what is missing.

### What it builds
- **A project column**, which is the one he asked for first. Show the project by NAME rather than a full path, since a path in a table column is unreadable and the projects table already holds a name; the full path belongs on hover.
- **Started and last active.** `created_at` and `last_seen` are already stored. Draw them as an AGE a person can read at a glance rather than a raw timestamp, in the shape the rest of this pane already uses; the exact time belongs on hover. Say plainly in the phase what `last_seen` actually means, because it is the manifest's own liveness stamp rather than a record of the person's last keystroke, and a column labelled last active must not claim more than the field knows.
- **Both new columns SORT**, because Phase 170 made every table in this pane sortable at his instruction and a new column that does not sort is a regression. `SessionSortCol` at `src/renderer/diagnostics/format.ts:195` is the union to extend, and its sort function is the thing to extend with it.
- Under Just enough words: short column headers, no explanatory paragraph, the detail on hover.

### What it must get right
- **A row with no manifest match still draws.** A session Tortie did not launch, or one whose manifest row is gone, shows the columns empty rather than vanishing from the table or drawing a guess. Losing a row would be worse than the missing column.
- **The table stays live.** Phase 170 made these tables sample live while the pane is visible at his instruction, so the new columns keep up rather than being right only at open.
- **No new spawn, no new sampling, no new poll.** Every value comes from state Tortie already holds.

### Proof, run rather than read
- ONE app run over a real manifest with MANY sessions, since his screenshot has dozens: every row carries a project or an honest blank, the ages read correctly, both new columns sort in both directions, and the repeated names are now distinguishable.
- THE NAMED INDEPENDENT METHOD: re-derive the project and both timestamps for a sample of rows by reading the manifest directly with your own query, and prove the drawn values match. The table agreeing with the code that fills it proves nothing.
- The parent measurement: at the parent, show two rows with the same name and no way to tell them apart; at HEAD, show the same two rows distinguished.
- A row whose manifest entry is missing, proved to draw with empty columns rather than disappearing.
- The battery.

### What is NOT in this phase
- No new measurement, sampling, poll or spawn.
- No change to the process table, the glance strip or anything else Phase 170 built.
- No filtering, grouping or searching of the sessions table; columns only.
- No change to how sessions are named.

## Phase 189 — a project tab you cannot read is not a tab (operator reported 2026-08-31)

**Subject:** `fix(titlebar): project tabs stay readable when there are too many`
**First body line:** `Phase 189: the tabs you cannot read`
**Semver:** minor if a scrolling or overflow affordance is added, patch if it is only a fitting rule.
**Tier 2**, one app run across widths and project counts, one named independent method. He reported it, so the PARENT MEASUREMENT IS MANDATORY.
**Charter:** his words and screenshot of 2026-08-31, wanting more tab information, or scrolling, when there are more horizontal project tabs than there is room for.

### What his screenshot actually shows, and it is worse than crowding
Twelve projects on one row. The names have been squeezed past the point of meaning: `g...`, `d..`, `h...`, `roo...`, `runs...`, `tortied...`. Only the active tab is readable at all. A tab whose label is one letter and an ellipsis identifies nothing, so the row costs its whole height and returns almost no information. One tab also shows an orange `Greg's Ma` badge, so a machine mark competes for the same squeezed space and must be part of whatever rule is chosen.

### The tree, read before this was queued
`src/renderer/app/Titlebar.tsx` draws the row of tabs in the top orientations, about 482 lines, and its own header records the three layouts: projects on top expanded is the row of tabs, projects on the left is no tabs at all because `ProjectRail.tsx` draws them instead. What each tab holds is derived in `./project-tabs-data.ts`. The left rail already solves the same problem a different way, with `overflow-y: auto` in `project-rail.css`, so THE APP ALREADY SCROLLS PROJECTS in one orientation and this phase makes the other honest. Confirm all of this against the tree first.

### The decision the phase must make, and it is a decision rather than a detail
Three answers are possible and the phase picks ONE with a reason, rather than doing several:
1. **Scroll the row**, which is what he named first and what the left rail already does. Then a tab keeps a readable minimum width and the row scrolls horizontally past it, with some affordance saying there is more.
2. **Overflow into a menu**, the way the session tab strip already handles its own crowding with a chevron, which keeps one row and no scrolling and reuses a pattern the app already has.
3. **A floor with honest truncation**, where a tab never shrinks below a width at which its name is still recognisable, and what does not fit goes to whichever of 1 or 2 is chosen.
The floor in 3 is needed by BOTH 1 and 2, so measure it first: the width at which a real project name stops being identifiable, taken from his own project names rather than invented. **Whatever is chosen, a tab must never again be drawn as one letter and an ellipsis.**

### What it must get right
- **The machine badge.** A tab carrying a machine mark needs room for it or a different way to show it; the badge must not be what squeezes the name.
- **The active tab keeps its advantage.** It is the one a person needs to read most and it is readable today; do not regress it to win uniformity.
- **The digit chords still reach.** The Titlebar header records that holding command reveals the digit that reaches each tab, command 1 to 8 by position and command 9 the last, in `project-shortcuts.ts`. If a tab can now be scrolled out of view or hidden in a menu, say what the chord does then, and prove it still works.
- **Reordering by pointer drag still works**, since the header records tabs reorder by a shared drag engine, and a scrolling container is exactly where drag-to-reorder breaks.
- The left rail orientation is NOT changed; it already works.

### Proof, run rather than read
- THE PARENT MEASUREMENT: at the parent, with his own twelve projects open at his own window width, record the drawn label of every tab and show how many are unidentifiable; at HEAD, the same drive showing every tab either readable or honestly reachable. Numbers, not adjectives.
- One app run across at least three window widths and at least three project counts, including two and twelve, reading the drawn labels and widths at each.
- THE NAMED INDEPENDENT METHOD: measure the readability floor yourself off the DOM, being the width each real project name needs before it truncates to nothing, rather than taking the component's belief for it.
- Drive the whole journey: open and close projects while narrow, and resize live, proving the row keeps up rather than being right only at mount, which is the lesson that caught 175, 181, 174.1, 181.1 and 181.2.
- The digit chord and pointer reorder both proved still working under the new rule.
- The battery.

### What is NOT in this phase
- No change to the left rail orientation.
- No change to what a tab holds beyond what the fitting rule needs; project tab CONTENT is `project-tabs-data.ts` and is not redesigned here.
- No new setting for tab width or layout.
- No change to the session tab strip, which Phase 181.1 just settled.

## Phase 174.2 — the font field sits level with its own dropdown (operator reported 2026-08-31)

**Subject:** `fix(settings): the custom font field lines up with the select beside it`
**First body line:** `Phase 174.2: the field sits level`
**Semver:** patch.
**Tier 2**, and small, but the PARENT MEASUREMENT IS MANDATORY because he reported it and because the last phase to touch this row traded one defect for another.
**Charter:** his words and screenshot of 2026-08-31: on Settings then Appearance, the Terminal and editor font row, the Custom text field and the Custom dropdown beside it are not aligned vertically. His screenshot shows the field sitting visibly HIGHER than the select.

### The cause, read from the tree, and it is Phase 174.1's own fix
`.set-font-custom` at `src/renderer/settings/settings.css:184` is a COLUMN flex holding two children: the input, and the not installed note. Phase 174.1 made that note occupy its line ALWAYS, hidden by `visibility` rather than `display`, so the field would stop being shoved upward while a person types in it. That fix was right and it must not be undone. But the row centres its controls, and this control is now two rows tall while the select beside it is one, so centring the COLUMN puts its first row, the input, above the select's centre line. The misalignment is the exact width of half the reserved note.

### The rule that decides the fix, and both halves must hold
1. **The input's box lines up with the select's box**, top and bottom, at rest and while typing.
2. **The input does not move when the note appears or goes.** That is Phase 174.1's promise and it is why the note is reserved rather than conditional. A fix that recentres the column on the note appearing has reintroduced the defect he reported before.
Achieve both by taking the note out of the input's own layout while keeping its space reserved, whichever way the tree makes honest: the note positioned beneath the field rather than stacked above it in flow, or the column aligned so the INPUT rather than the column is what the row centres. Do not solve it by removing the reservation.

### Proof, run rather than read
- THE PARENT MEASUREMENT: at the parent, read the input's and the select's rectangles off the DOM and report the vertical offset between them in pixels, which his screenshot says is not zero; at HEAD, show it is zero or within a pixel. Numbers, not adjectives.
- THE SAME MEASUREMENT WITH THE NOTE SPEAKING and with it silent, proving the input's rectangle is IDENTICAL in both, which is Phase 174.1's guard and the thing this fix could break.
- One app run driving the whole journey, being switch to Custom, type a real family, type a family that is not installed so the note speaks, correct it, clear the field, and switch back to a preset, reading the rectangles at every step.
- The 174.1 probe still green, and if this ships a guard it goes red at the parent and is NAMED in package.json and build/verification-checks.mjs.
- The battery.

### What is NOT in this phase
- No change to the suggestion list, the availability measurement or the copy.
- No change to any other Settings row, and no new token.
- The reservation of the note's line is NOT removed.

## Phase 190 — the four inline modes are three, on a pure deletion (research 74, operator asked 2026-09-01)

**Subject:** `fix(diff): the inline control says what it can tell apart`
**First body line:** `Phase 190: three outcomes wearing four names`
**Semver:** patch.
**Tier 2**, one app run over a fixture carrying both a deletion and a replacement, one named independent method.
**Charter:** this entry plus docs/research/74-redline-in-the-diff-view.md. Research 74 measured, on HIS OWN test file, that the Phase 185 four way Inline control has only TWO outcomes: Words, Phrases and Characters draw BYTE IDENTICAL markup, md5 c11388b3 stacked and 7c5465f9 split. This is what he actually saw when he changed the control and nothing happened.

### The cause, measured rather than guessed, and it is not Tortie's
Research 74 re-derived it in node against the INSTALLED jsdiff: `diffWords`, `diffWordsWithSpace` and `diffChars` all return the same three parts on his pair, because his edit is a pure word DELETION with nothing inserted, so there is nothing for a finer grain to divide. The cause is upstream of Pierre and of Tortie, and NOTHING IS BROKEN. The defect is that the control offers four names for what is sometimes one answer and says nothing about it, so a person changes it, sees no change, and concludes the feature does not work. That is exactly what happened.

### The decision this phase makes, and it is a copy and behaviour decision rather than a diff one
Pick ONE with a reason and do not do several:
1. **Say nothing and change nothing.** Defensible: the modes are honest, and a replacement shows the difference plainly. But he already hit this once and it read as broken.
2. **Say it on the face when it is true.** When the drawn markup for the chosen mode is identical to what a coarser mode would draw, one short line says the modes agree on this change. Honest and quiet, and it costs a comparison per render.
3. **Disable what cannot differ.** Grey the modes that would draw the same thing for the hunks on screen. Truthful but it makes a control flicker as a person scrolls, which is worse.
**Measure the cost of 2 before choosing it**, because comparing renders per change is not free, and if it is expensive then 1 with a documentation line is the honest answer. Under Just enough words: at most one short line, no paragraph, nothing on the resting face when the modes DO differ.

### Proof, run rather than read
- A fixture carrying BOTH shapes: a pure deletion, where the modes agree, and a replacement, where Words, Phrases and Characters must draw measurably different markup. Report the span counts for all four modes on both, so the difference and the sameness are both numbers.
- THE NAMED INDEPENDENT METHOD: re-derive the parts by calling the installed jsdiff yourself on both fixtures, and prove the drawn markup follows what the library returned rather than what the control promised.
- If option 2 ships, measure what the comparison costs on a large diff and say the number.
- The battery.

### What is NOT in this phase
- No change to the four modes themselves, their names, or what they draw when they do differ.
- No redline; that is Phase 191.
- No new diff library and no change to which functions are called.

## Phase 191 — a change reads like a redline (research 74, operator asked 2026-09-01)

**Subject:** `feat(diff): a change can read as a redline`
**First body line:** `Phase 191: struck through, then replaced`
**Semver:** minor.
**Tier 2**, one app run driving the whole journey, one named independent method; escalate to Tier 3 if it lands anywhere that spawns or persists.
**Charter:** this entry plus docs/research/74-redline-in-the-diff-view.md, and his Wordie screenshot of 2026-08-31: the deleted words struck through in red IMMEDIATELY FOLLOWED by the inserted words, inline, the way a person marks up a document.

### What research 74 settled, so no round re-derives it
- **PIERRE CANNOT DRAW IT, and the reason is structural rather than a missing option.** Its `[data-content]` is `display: grid` with `grid-template-rows: subgrid`, so every diff line is a grid item whose display is BLOCKIFIED by the CSS specification. Forcing `display: inline !important` into Pierre's own shadow root in the running app left the display `block` while the colour and the strikethrough in the same rule both took, and its 39,124 character stylesheet carries zero `!important` declarations, so there is no cascade to win.
- **PIERRE CAN HOLD IT.** `lineAnnotations` and `renderAnnotation` are exported and supported, their content lands in the LIGHT DOM with `white-space: normal` already set and tokens.css reaching it, and in STACKED mode `DiffHunksRenderer.js` merges both sides into ONE annotation row. Research 73 was too absolute in saying otherwise.
- **TORTIE CAN DRAW IT, and it was rendered.** One div of span, del and ins held four deletions and four insertions in ONE element, insertion immediately after deletion on the same line, coloured from `--error` and `--success` with NO new token, reflowing 20px to 60px when squeezed.
- **THE LIBRARY IS ALREADY HERE.** `diff` 9.0.0 BSD-3-Clause is a production dependency with `@pierre/diffs` as its only dependent; importing `diffWords` costs 3,389 raw and 1,056 gzip in the lazy EditorPanel chunk. No new package.

### THE FIRST STEP, and the phase does it before anything else
**Prove the annotation slot in ONE app run.** It is the only claim in research 74 read from source rather than run. Mount a trivial annotation row in stacked mode in the real app and read it off the DOM. If it holds, the redline is an annotation row in stacked mode. If it does not, the redline is a Redline mode on the markdown tab, which is research 73's recommendation and still stands. THE PHASE PICKS ITS HOME FROM THAT MEASUREMENT rather than from either document.

### What it builds
- Tortie's own React `del` and `ins` over `diffWords`, drawn as ONE flowing line per changed pair, from tokens only.
- **A COPY HANDLER IS REQUIRED, not optional.** Research 74 measured that selection interleaves the two sides verbatim, so a person copying a redlined region gets the old and new text mixed. Decide what copy yields and implement it; leaving it is shipping a defect.
- Where it lives is the first step's answer, and it is a MODE a person chooses rather than a replacement for what the diff view does today.
- Under Just enough words: one short label, no explanation on the resting face.

### What it must get right
- **A multi line change.** Three lines deleted and one inserted is not one pair, and the phase says what it draws rather than pretending.
- **Syntax highlighting fights it.** A code diff is coloured by token and a redline wants colour by change. Say which wins in redline mode and why.
- **Line numbers and the gutter.** If a redline merges two rows into one, say what number and what mark that row carries.
- **It may honestly be prose only.** His own case is a text file, and a redline in a syntax highlighted source file is arguably wrong. If the phase concludes prose only, that is a real answer.

### Proof, run rather than read
- The annotation slot proved or refuted in one app run FIRST, and the home chosen from it.
- A rendered redline over a fixture that REPLACES words, since research 74 warns that on a pure deletion a redline and a plain strikethrough are the same picture in any implementation including Word's, so a deletion fixture cannot show the feature works.
- THE NAMED INDEPENDENT METHOD: re-derive the runs by calling jsdiff yourself and compare them to the drawn del and ins ranges read off the DOM.
- The copy handler proved by reading what the clipboard actually receives, not by reading the code.
- Drive the whole journey: switch modes with a diff open, scroll, resize, and open a second file.
- The battery, and if a guard ships it goes red at the parent and is NAMED in package.json and build/verification-checks.mjs.

### What is NOT in this phase
- No change to the four inline modes, which are Phase 190.
- No accept and reject affordance; his reference app has Accept All and Reject All and this phase refuses both, because accepting a change means WRITING A FILE and that is a different feature with different risks.
- No new package.
- No change to split mode if the slot answer is stacked only.

## Research 75 — a visual language for the chrome, with options he can look at (operator asked 2026-09-01)

**Subject:** `docs(research): a visual language update for the app chrome`
**First body line:** `Research 75: the chrome, made premium`
**Charter:** his words of 2026-09-01. He wants the FULL APP CHROME made more premium, being the lines, the typography, the weights of the icons, slight fades and colouring, and the edges, which he likes and wants kept. **NOT A REARRANGEMENT.** Nothing moves. He named VS Code's recent repaint and a Ghostty terminal as inspiration and said he PARTICULARLY LIKES THE GHOSTTY ONE. He asked for a lot of research, for the best interfaces to be studied rather than guessed at, and for A FEW OPTIONS WRITTEN FOR HIS REVIEW WITH MOCKS, and he asked for it to be thought about deeply.

### The one rule that decides whether a proposal is any good
**It must speak to the soul of docs/ZEN-OF-TORTIE.md.** A visual language that could belong to any editor is decoration and fails. Read the Zen FIRST, and every proposal names which of its beliefs it is expressing and how. Tortie already has beliefs a look can carry: the glance answers who needs me, so attention has to be the loudest thing on screen and nothing else may compete with it; just enough words, so the chrome says little and says it quietly; sessions are durable and the app is disposable, so the chrome should feel like a calm frame around work that outlives it.

### What is IN scope, in his own words
Lines and hairlines, typography and its weights, icon weight and consistency, slight fades, colour and its restraint, edges and radii, elevation, the resting versus active distinction, and the contrast relationship between chrome and content.

### What is OUT, and this is absolute
- **Nothing moves.** No layout, no rearrangement, no new surface, no removed surface, no changed information architecture. If a proposal needs something to move, it is the wrong proposal.
- No new package, no icon set replacement unless the survey proves the current set is the defect and even then it is a recorded option rather than a decision.
- No change to what any surface SAYS.

### What the research must actually do, rather than assert
1. **Read the soul and the standing design law**, being docs/ZEN-OF-TORTIE.md, DESIGN.md, docs/DESIGN-SPEC.md, and say what is already decided and may not be reopened.
2. **MEASURE THE CHROME AS IT IS.** src/renderer/styles/tokens.css is 374 lines and app.css is 2,490; report the real inventory, being every border colour and width, every radius, every font size and weight, the icon sizes and stroke weights actually drawn, the spacing scale, and every place the app CONTRADICTS ITSELF today. The inconsistencies are the cheapest wins and they are findable rather than arguable.
3. **STUDY THE REFERENCES MECHANICALLY**, being his two images plus the best interfaces available to study, and report MEASURABLE mechanics rather than adjectives: the contrast distance between chrome text and content text, how hairlines are drawn, the radius family and whether inner and outer radii nest, icon stroke weight consistency, how many type sizes are in use and whether hierarchy comes from weight and colour instead of size, how elevation is expressed without drop shadows, what is allowed to be the one bright thing, and where fades are used to say there is more.
4. **NAME WHAT A REPAINT COSTS.** Many probes photograph the app and compare pixels; a chrome change moves them. Count them and say which. The `gmux-*` CSS classes are load bearing per CLAUDE.md and are never renamed. Say what the Pierre diff theme bridge and the xterm palette inherit, because a token change reaches them.
5. **THREE OPTIONS, each internally coherent**, each expressed as a TOKEN DIFF a phase could apply, each naming the Zen belief it carries, each with its risks and what it would break, and each with A MOCK HE CAN LOOK AT.

### The mocks, and they are the deliverable he asked for
Each option gets a self contained HTML file under docs/research/assets/75-chrome/ reproducing TORTIE'S OWN CHROME at its real proportions, being the title bar with project tabs, the activity rail, the sidebar, the session tab strip, the terminal area and the status bar, drawn with that option's tokens. Use his own real content from his screenshots so he recognises it. No external asset, no network request, no framework; inline CSS only. The mocks exist to be COMPARED, so all three carry the same content and differ only in the visual language, and one further file shows the CURRENT chrome the same way as the control. A mock that cannot be set beside the others is useless.

### What is NOT in this document
- No queued phase. He reads the options and picks, and only then does a phase get written.
- No change to any product file. The research writes its document and its mocks and nothing else.

## Phase 192: the skills sheet is too wide and the preview too short

**Subject.** `fix(install): the skills sheet stops taking the whole window`

**First body line.** `Phase 192: the skills sheet is narrower and its preview taller`

**Semver.** PATCH. Nothing is added, removed or renamed. Two numbers move on one
existing modal and a third stops being flat. No setting, no new surface, no menu change.

**Tier 2, and the parent measurement is MANDATORY** because he reported it personally. It is a
rendered surface with no new state, so one app run drives every claim. The independent method,
named before the work starts, is **attack rather than confirm**: the phase will conclude the sheet
is narrower and the preview taller, and the verifier's job is to try to break that at the viewport
where Phase 132's regression lives, being 586 px with six acknowledgement rows in the control band,
re-deriving the Install button's hit test itself rather than re-running the builder's probe
invocation and reading its verdict.

**Charter.** His words on 2026-09-01 with two screenshots, the search step and the preview step:
reduce the size of the skills search and results slightly, give the preview more height or allow for
total scroll, "we've changed this before but now its just too wide and isn't aesthetically
pleasing".

### THIS REVERSES HIS OWN EARLIER RULING, AND THE COMMENT MUST SAY SO

`src/renderer/context/install/install.css:202` carries the reason the sheet is 1600 px wide, and the
reason is him: *"Widened in Phase 132 from 880px to 1120px, and again on 2026-08-23 when the
operator asked for the sheet to take up more of the screen."* That comment is now wrong about what
he wants, and a later round reading it will widen the sheet back. The comment is rewritten in this
phase, dated 2026-09-01, saying plainly that he asked for it wide and then asked for it narrower
after living with it, and that the second word is the current one. Deleting the history is not
allowed; the record of both rulings is what stops the third round.

### THE TRAP, AND IT IS THE WHOLE PHASE

`.ctx-install-sheet` at `install.css:211` reads `width: min(1600px, 92vw)`. **At his window the
1600 px cap never binds.** His screenshots are 2970 and 2948 device pixels wide at 2x, so his window
is about 1485 logical px, and 92vw of that is about 1366 px. A phase that lowers 1600 to 1280 and
stops changes NOTHING on his machine and he reports it again. The number he is actually looking at
is the `92vw`.

So the first thing this phase does is measure, in the running app at his own window size, which of
the two terms is binding, and the fix moves the term that is. My arithmetic above is from a
screenshot and is not evidence; the app run replaces it.

### WHAT MOVES

1. **The sheet's width**, `install.css:211`. The binding term comes down. There is a hard floor and
   it is not taste: `install.css:384` is `@container ctxd-preview (min-width: 680px)`, and below
   that the preview collapses from two columns to one, which makes the sheet TALLER and makes his
   second complaint worse. The chosen width is stated with the measured margin it leaves above that
   680 px container, at his window and at a 1280 px one.

2. **Band 3, the skill's own text**, `install.css:536`, `max-height: calc(var(--space-10) * 3)`,
   being 144 px, which after 16 px of padding on each side is the 6 visible lines in his second
   screenshot. This is the box he wants taller. A flat 144 px is the defect: it refuses the room a
   tall window already has. It becomes a bound that grows with the sheet and keeps 144 px as its
   floor, so a small window is exactly what it is today and a tall one is not.

3. **Nothing else in the band stack**, and specifically NOT `install.css:495`, the 144 px floor on
   band 1. Its own comment says *"DO NOT RAISE THIS without driving the six row stress in the
   probe"*, and 192 px was already specified, driven and rejected once at Phase 132.1. This phase
   does not touch it.

### WHAT "TOTAL SCROLL" MEANS HERE, AND WHY THE LITERAL READING IS REFUSED

He offered making the whole thing scroll as an alternative. One scroller for the whole sheet is
exactly what Phase 132 removed, and the numbers are in the comment at `install.css:214`: the sheet
was one scroller 2097 px tall with the Install button 776 px down inside it, so at a 700 px window
the button sat 128 px past the bottom edge and at 586 px it sat 242 px past. The button is the
thing the sheet exists for. His intent, being that he can reach all of the preview text, is met by
band 3 growing and continuing to scroll inside itself. The entry records the refusal with those
numbers so it is a decision rather than an omission, and the phase says it back to him in the
report.

### WHAT ELSE THE COMMIT MUST CARRY

`src/renderer/context/install/__tests__/install-layout.test.ts:191` asserts the width string contains
`1600px` and `92vw`, and lines 217 and 220 pin both `calc(var(--space-10) * 3)` rules. Those
assertions are updated in the SAME commit to the new numbers, still as text read out of the
stylesheet, or the phase lands red. A test that pins the old number is not a test that was left
behind, it is the gate that catches this drifting back.

### PROOF, RUN RATHER THAN READ

One app run, launched through `build/electron-run.mjs` on its own userData, driving the whole
journey rather than a resting state: open Context, type a query, get results, open a result, reach
the preview.

- The sheet's measured width in CSS px at the parent commit and at HEAD, at his own window size and
  at 1280 px and at 700 px, with which term of the `min()` was binding at each.
- The preview container's measured width at HEAD against the 680 px container query, proving the two
  column layout survives.
- Band 3's visible content height and its scrollHeight at parent and at HEAD on a tall window, and
  the same on a short one showing the floor held.
- **The Phase 132 stress, at parent and at HEAD**: a 586 px viewport with six acknowledgement rows,
  the Install button's bottom edge against the sheet's bottom edge as two numbers, and
  `document.elementFromPoint` at the button's own centre returning the button. `npm run probe:p132`
  drives this; the verifier re-derives it independently rather than reading the probe's verdict.
- Gates: `npm run typecheck && npm run build && npm run smoke:t1` plus `npm test`, and
  `build/assert-css-order.mjs` runs inside the build.

### What is NOT in this phase

- **The install confirm is not touched.** `.ctxd-install-modal` at `install.css:36` is 1120 px and is
  a DIFFERENT surface, drawn by `InstallDialog.tsx:109`, and it appears in neither screenshot. Its
  width exists so the command line being approved is one line rather than three, which is a
  correctness reason rather than a taste one. It stays.
- **Nothing is rearranged.** The two column preview from Phase 26 keeps its columns, its 5fr to 7fr
  split and its order. No band changes places.
- **Nothing changes about what the sheet SHOWS.** No field added, no field removed, no copy
  rewritten, no facts section reworded. The 300 character description slice in `install-store.ts`
  stays as it is.
- **No sheet-wide scroller**, for the reason above.
- **Not the Context panel behind it**, being its filter field, its SKILLS group or its counts.
- **Nothing about what runs.** `install-gate.ts`, the confirm hash and the command composition are

- **`app.css` is not edited**, which is the same rule Phase 132 kept.
- **No native menu change**, because no surface is added, renamed or removed.

## Phase 193: a harness run must not be able to write in his known_hosts

**Subject.** `fix(harness): a probe cannot write a line in the person's known_hosts`

**First body line.** `Phase 193: the harness keeps its host keys to itself`

**Semver.** PATCH. Nothing user facing changes. This is the test harness and a new gate.

**Tier 3.** It touches ssh, it writes in a file under the person's home, and the rule it enforces
already exists for the product. The evidence is a reproduction in a scratch HOME plus a scan proved
on fixtures, and the independent methods are **re-derive** and **attack**.

**Charter.** Phase 187's committer reported it rather than acting on it, which was the right call:
`~/.ssh/known_hosts` measured **2,120 bytes holding 3 entries for `127.0.0.1`** on 2026-09-01, and it
could not attribute them to a particular run. Confirmed independently the same night at the same
2,120 bytes and the same 3 entries. CLAUDE.md already records the same file at 932 bytes before a
probe run and 1,229 after, during the machines work, so harness runs leaving loopback lines in his
file is a known shape rather than a guess.

### Why this is a real defect and not housekeeping

The product side is already correct and already gated. `src/main/machines/ssh.ts:277` and `:316` carry
`StrictHostKeyChecking=yes` with `UserKnownHostsFile=` set, and `npm run conformance:machines` asserts
that the connection test argv names Tortie's own host key file FIRST and the person's second. That
gate exists **because the product once added three lines to his `~/.ssh/known_hosts`**, measured at
932 bytes before and 1,229 after.

The harness has no such gate. Several scripts do scope it, being
`build/capture-machine-goldens.mjs:232`, `build/p118-remote-children.mjs:297`,
`build/probe-control-dialect.mjs:250` and `build/probe-control-deadline.mjs:171`. Whether every script
that can reach ssh does is UNKNOWN, and unknown is the finding. A probe that writes in his
`~/.ssh` is the same defect the product gate was written to end, arriving through the back door.

### What the phase does

1. **Find it by reproduction, not by reading.** Run the machine-touching probes with `HOME` pointed at
   a scratch directory and compare that scratch `known_hosts` before and after, byte for byte. The
   script or scripts that write a line are then named by evidence rather than by inspection. Reading
   the tree for a missing option is the cheap first pass; the reproduction is what settles it, because
   a script can reach ssh through a helper that adds options of its own.
2. **Fix it at the source.** Every harness path that runs ssh, `ssh-keyscan` or an sshd against
   loopback names its own host key file under its own scratch directory, the way
   `build/probe-control-dialect.mjs:250` already does. Prefer ONE shared helper over four call sites,
   the way `build/electron-run.mjs` owns every Electron launch, so a later script cannot forget.
3. **Gate it.** `npm run gate:knownhosts` scans every file under `build/` for a spawn whose program is
   ssh, scp, sftp or ssh-keyscan and fails when the argv does not scope `UserKnownHostsFile` to a path
   the script owns. It is named in `package.json` AND in `build/verification-checks.mjs`, it runs
   inside `npm run build` so nothing that builds can skip it, and **it proves its own scanner on
   fixtures it writes itself**, at least one of which must make it fail. A gate that cannot fail is
   not a gate.

### What it must NOT do, and this one is absolute

**His `~/.ssh/known_hosts` is not edited, not truncated, not rewritten and not backed up.** The three
loopback lines already in it stay exactly where they are. This phase stops new ones being written and
nothing else. If those lines should go, that is his to do, and the phase says so in its report rather
than doing it. Nothing anywhere under `~/.ssh` is written, moved or deleted.

### Proof, run rather than read

- **The reproduction, at the parent.** A scratch `HOME`, its `known_hosts` byte count before and after
  each machine-touching probe, naming which script grew it and by how many bytes and lines.
- **The same reproduction at HEAD**, showing zero growth for every one of them.
- **The gate proved red.** Run it against a fixture that omits the option and show it fails with the
  file and the reason named, then against the real tree and show it passes.
- **A byte count of his real `~/.ssh/known_hosts` before and after the whole phase, proving it is
  unchanged at 2,120 bytes.** Read only, both times.
- `npm run conformance:machines` still passes, so the product side did not move.
- The battery.

### What is NOT in this phase

- **No edit to any file under `~/.ssh`.** Reading a byte count is the only contact.
- **No change to the product's ssh layer.** `src/main/machines/**` is untouched. The product is
  already correct and already gated, and widening this phase into it is how a harness fix becomes a
  machines phase.
- **No new probe and no new coverage.** Existing scripts get their host key file scoped; none gains a
  capability.
- **Not the `known_hosts` of any remote machine**, and his Mac Pro is never contacted.
- **No change to `StrictHostKeyChecking` anywhere in the product**, which is `yes` and stays `yes`.

**The rule, and it binds every future round.**

1. **New things go at the BOTTOM.** A new phase entry, a phase that starts, a phase that lands and
   a phase that is queued all get one line appended at the end of this section, newest last. Never
   reorder this section and never rewrite a line in it once the event has happened.
2. **An old entry may still be edited in place**, and this is the exception the operator named. A
   phase that was written down earlier but never queued can be updated where it sits when it is
   finally queued, because its reasoning belongs beside the entries it relates to. That is an edit
   to an existing entry rather than a new thing.
3. **Every phase still gets a FULL SECTION in the house shape, and that never changes.** The log
   is an index, not a replacement, and a one line entry is never enough to build from. A new phase
   is written the way the hundred phases above it are written, with all of these: a `## Phase N`
   heading naming the defect or the capability in the operator's words, the **Subject** line for
   the commit, the **First body line** carrying the phase label, the **Semver**, the **Tier** with
   the reason that tier was chosen, the **Charter** naming the entry and any research document that
   binds it, the mechanism written out with the real file paths read from the tree, the proof the
   phase must produce run rather than read, and a **What is NOT in this phase** section, because
   the refusals are what stop a later round widening the work. A phase entered as a single line has
   not been queued, it has been mentioned.
4. **A new phase section is APPENDED at the end too**, immediately above this log, so the file
   grows downward and the newest work is always the last thing before the log. The log stays the
   final section of the file.
5. **The log is one line per event**, being the date, what happened, and the hash and version when
   it landed.
